summary: This sample is the Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu (at.%) "17Al" low-density steel in the state produced by solution treatment at 1100 °C for 10 min under argon followed by oil quenching, then aging at 625 °C for 3 h and water quenching. It belongs to a study of how Al content (15, 17, 19 at.%) controls the aging-hardening behaviour of Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels hardened by the ultra-hard β-Mn phase. After 3 h at 625 °C the alloy is essentially a β-Mn matrix carrying fine BCC and FCC Cu-rich precipitates, and shows a Vickers hardness of 872.0 ± 24.4 HV versus a solution-treated baseline of 259.8 ± 1.5 HV.
composition: Nominal composition Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu (at.%), one of a series with x = 15, 17, 19 at.% Al. EDS-measured chemistry of the 17Al alloy: Fe 43.2, Mn 34.8, Al 17.0, Cu 5.0 at.%; the Al variation across the series is achieved essentially by substituting Al for Fe, while Mn (~34.8 at.%) and Cu (~5 at.%) stay constant. Fe is the base element; the high Mn level (35 at.%) was chosen to promote precipitation kinetics of hard β-Mn, Al is the primary density-reducing element (about 0.1 g/cm³ per 1 wt.% Al) and also influences β-Mn precipitation and hardening, and Cu was added (as in the authors' earlier Fe-Mn-Al-Cu alloy) to accelerate β-Mn precipitation and raise hardness. Density measured by the Archimedes method is 6.76 g/cm³.
processing: Alloy ingots of nominal Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu (at.%) were melted from raw materials of high purity (>99.9 %) in a vacuum induction furnace under an argon atmosphere. Ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h and then hot-rolled into plates 4 mm thick, from which 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ samples were cut by electrical discharge machining for hardness testing and microstructural characterization. The parent (precursor) process of this sample is a solution treatment at 1100 °C for 10 min under an argon atmosphere followed by oil quenching, which produces a single-phase α (BCC) matrix. The defining step of this sample is aging at 625 °C for 3 h followed by water quenching, drawn from the general aging schedule of 525–650 °C for 1, 3, 6 and 10 h. Specimens were prepared by electrolytic polishing in 10 % perchloric acid + 90 % ethanol.
microstructure: After aging at 625 °C for 3 h the 17Al alloy consists essentially of a β-Mn (cubic β-Mn) matrix with near-equiaxed matrix grains, in which numerous fine new precipitates are dispersed: a new BCC phase located within the β-Mn (between β-Mn interfaces) and an FCC Cu-rich phase located at the β-Mn interfaces. Three phases are thus present (β-Mn, new BCC phase, FCC Cu-rich phase). The α → β-Mn transformation is nearly complete because for the 17Al alloy the α (BCC) matrix almost completely transforms to β-Mn within just 1 h at 600 °C and above, after 6 h at 550 °C, and only slowly at 525 °C (about 20.5 % β-Mn after 10 h). Reports of α-Mn particles coexisting with β-Mn during aging and of FCC twins inside the Cu-rich particles come from other conditions of the same alloy (e.g. 525 °C/10 h, 575 °C/6 h TEM); the 625 °C/3 h condition itself was not separately imaged. Microstructure evolution sequence for these alloys: α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase.
properties: Vickers hardness (HVS-1000 tester, 9.8 N for 15 s, average of 5 measurements): 872.0 ± 24.4 HV, versus 259.8 ± 1.5 HV for the solution-treated 17Al baseline. For this alloy, hardness at 625 °C varies only weakly with time (813.0 ± 20.8 HV at 1 h, 872.0 ± 24.4 HV at 3 h, 878.4 ± 28.3 HV at 6 h, 870.5 ± 24.9 HV at 10 h), and the overall 17Al aging window spans 259.8–924.9 HV, with the peak (924.9 ± 25.8 HV) reached at 575 °C for 6 h. Young's modulus reported for the 17Al alloy is 175 GPa. Density is 6.76 g/cm³; the paper reports a maximum specific hardness of 141 HV·cm³/g for the 15Al alloy, based on the ultra-wide 253.4–965.6 HV range across the series. Characterization techniques applied across the alloy series: Vickers microhardness testing, X-ray diffraction (D8 Discover), secondary-electron SEM imaging and EDS (ZEISS Sigma 300, 5 kV), EBSD (GeminiSEM 300; step sizes 1.5 μm and 0.05 μm), TEM bright/dark-field imaging, SAED, HRTEM and FFT with EDS (FEI Talos F200X, 200 kV), and nanoindentation (Agilent G200, 200 nm depth).
mechanisms: Aging drives the transformation α (BCC) → β-Mn, and because β-Mn has a very high intrinsic hardness (over 10 GPa; 12.2 ± 0.1 GPa measured by nanoindentation for the hardest 17Al condition), the extensive formation of β-Mn is the origin of the alloy's ultra-high hardness.

For the 17Al alloy the transformation is fast at high temperature: at 600 °C and above the α matrix has almost completely transformed to β-Mn within only 1 h, so by 625 °C/3 h the matrix is essentially β-Mn and hardness has already plateaued near 872 HV.

Increasing Al content slows the precipitation kinetics of β-Mn relative to 15Al because β-Mn is a Mn-rich phase whose nucleation and growth must expel large amounts of other atoms; more Al in solution enriches Al around β-Mn and hinders its further precipitation and growth (hence 17Al needs 6 h at 550 °C versus 3 h at 525 °C for 15Al).

Al also stabilizes and increases the amount and size of the Al-rich D0₃ phase; because β-Mn precipitation requires prior depletion of D0₃, a higher Al level indirectly retards β-Mn nucleation and growth.

The formation of the new BCC phase at the β-Mn interfaces is attributed to enrichment of the BCC-stabilizing element Al around those interfaces as Mn-rich β-Mn grows and expels Fe, Al and Cu into the surroundings.

The FCC Cu-rich phase forms at the β-Mn interfaces because of the limited solubility of Cu in Fe-based alloys and the expulsion of Cu from β-Mn during its precipitation and growth; FCC twins are frequently observed inside these Cu-rich particles.

Increasing Al raises the amount of FCC Cu-rich and BCC precipitates between β-Mn interfaces while decreasing the FCC Cu-rich fraction relative to BCC; since both precipitates are softer than β-Mn (nanoindentation values spread and drop when the indenter hits them), the absolute volume fraction of β-Mn falls and the overall hardness decreases with increasing Al content.

The increase in Al content slightly enhances the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn through solid-solution strengthening (Al in β-Mn rises from 14.3 at.% for 15Al to 16.3 at.% for 17Al to 17.5 at.% for 19Al), but this gain is minimal and is outweighed by the loss of β-Mn volume fraction.

Fracture toughness decreases with increasing Al content both because the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn rises and because the more ductile FCC Cu-rich phase (which is softer and more deformable than the BCC phase) becomes less abundant.
conclusions: Aging at 625 °C for 3 h places the 17Al alloy in the high-temperature regime where the α → β-Mn transformation is essentially complete while hardness has reached a stable plateau of about 870 HV, just below the alloy's peak of 924.9 HV obtained at 575 °C/6 h. The study as a whole shows that simple short-time aging of Fe-35Mn-xAl-5Cu (x = 15, 17, 19) low-density steels yields an ultra-wide, tunable hardness window from 253.4 HV to 965.6 HV, attributed to continuous precipitation of ultra-hard β-Mn; the 15Al alloy reaches the highest specific hardness of 141 HV·cm³/g. Increasing Al lowers density but slows β-Mn precipitation, shifts the optimal aging window to higher temperatures (about 550–600 °C for 17Al, 575–625 °C for 19Al) and reduces the peak hardness and fracture toughness. These alloys can be shaped in the soft solution-treated state and then aged to the required hardness ("one type of material, multiple uses"), which could cut the cost of producing hard, wear-resistant components; the remaining challenge is the trade-off between hardness and toughness.
unmapped: The detailed TEM evidence for FCC Cu-rich precipitates with FCC twins and for the β-Mn/FCC Cu-rich interface (EDS maps, SAED, HRTEM/FFT) was obtained on the 17Al alloy aged at 575 °C for 6 h (its hardest condition, 924.9 HV), not on the 625 °C/3 h sample; the 625 °C/3 h condition itself was not separately imaged by TEM.

EBSD phase maps and the XRD traces that identify α/D0₃, α-Mn and β-Mn were taken on selected other conditions of the alloy series (e.g. 17Al at 525 °C/10 h, 575 °C/6 h, 650 °C/10 h; XRD on 17Al at 575 °C/1 h), so the phase-fraction values quoted for 17Al do not pertain specifically to the 625 °C/3 h treatment.

No tensile yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, elongation or fatigue/creep data are reported for this sample; the only reported mechanical loading data are hardness, nanoindentation (on the hardest conditions) and indentation-derived fracture toughness of the peak-hardness samples (8.6 MPa·m¹ᐟ² for 15Al, 6.6 MPa·m¹ᐟ² for 17Al, 3.5 MPa·m¹ᐟ² for 19Al).
A specific-hardness value for the 17Al alloy is not reported explicitly; the 141 HV·cm³/g figure belongs to the Fe-35.2Mn-15.0Al-5.2Cu alloy.
